title: All Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Weapon Locations
summary:
Castlevania games typically have relatively simple combat. You press a button and a whip, sword, or other weapon usually comes out swinging. It's not usually complex with combos outside of the Lords of Shadow era, with the series typically focused more on exploration than a thrilling set of moves.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse significantly changes these combat mechanics as Rose has access to seven weapon families, complete with buffs and perks. Each type has four different possible upgrades you can find on your journey, with subsequent weapons recovered from grand chests. To find the best weapons in this metroidvania, you'll occasionally need to think outside the box and find hidden rooms in seemingly unassuming passages.

All Castlevania: Belmont's Curse weapons

While you start with the humble Longsword, rather than the Vampire Killer whip a Belmont would typically wield to smite Dracula's monstrous army, Rose is proficient with seven different types. Here are all the weapons in the game and their locations:

Sword

The sword is a quick weapon type that will do more damage to enemies if they're hit immediately after a backdash or slide. You can also use the Arcane Whip on enemies with the sword equipped to dash through them when it connects.

Shortsword & Shield

These two weapons bridge attack and defense, with regular presses hitting enemies with the shortsword and holding down the attack button blocking attacks from Rose's front. Hold down the button long enough to charge up a shield-dashing attack. Attacking while using the Arcane Whip will execute a shield bash, swatting away enemies in the air.

Spear

This long-range weapon has both melee and ranged capabilities. Press the attack button to thrust the spear into the nearest foe. Hold down the button to aim with a reticle showing where it will land, and release it to fling it. The Arcane Whip attack is a pushing attack that makes foes stumble backward.

Gauntlets

Gauntlets are the fastest weapon type in the game, and every hit Rose dishes out makes them stronger. When grappling with the Arcane Whip, Rose can also launch her victim skyward for a potential aerial combo.

Greatsword

This heavy, powerful blade has a slow swinging speed, but you can charge up a stronger blow by holding down the attack button. Using the Arcane Whip with one equipped will execute the Blade Dive, crashing into foes.

Dual Blades

What's better than one sword? How about swiping two at once! You can extend the combo by pressing the attack button immediately after the previous hit connects with an enemy. Using the Arcane Whip with this weapon type makes Rose wildly swing her blades around her, dealing damage to anything in her path.

Whip

This specialist weapon of Vampire hunters does almost double damage when striking enemies at the tip of the whip. If you use the Arcane Whip ability with this weapon type equipped, Rose will dash toward the enemy and smash them with her whip.

title: While You Wait For The Phasmophobia Movie, Don’t Miss This Hidden Gem
summary:
An official Phasmophobia movie is on the way; we learned as much last summer. But what if I said you could watch something quite like Kinetic's ghostbusting co-op game right now? 

That's the elevator pitch I bring you, fellow horror fans, less than two weeks out from Halloween. The movie is Never After Dark, a gorgeously shot, cleverly creepy ghost story that Phasmophobia fans shouldn't miss.

Never After Dark tells the story of Airi, a young woman who can commune with ghosts. She works as a traveling intermediary between the dead and the living, convincing spirits to move on and freeing residents from their hauntings. But on her latest gig, she discovers she's taken on a much harder assignment. And wow, that assignment looked really familiar in such a fun way.

Never After Dark has been described as a "J-Horror revival" project, recalling the ghost stories frequently imported to the US from Japan at the turn of the 21st Century. Movies like Ringu, Pulse, Dark Water, and Ju-On: The Grudge were a big deal in Japan and earned a lot of praise (and remakes, for better or worse) here in the States, too. I've never been a big fan of the term J-Horror, but I can see how it works as shorthand for that particular bundle of films. 

Director Dave Boyle is an American, but he has spent much of his career making movies in and about Japan. Some of those aforementioned inspirations for Never After Dark are my favorites in the genre, and Boyle's new film does indeed feel like them at times, though I was more often struck by how much it felt like I was playing a round of Phasmophobia. Even Airi, who works alone most of the time, finds herself with a small group of other characters, like a solo player hopping into an open lobby in Phasmophobia. I won't spoil the movie, but suffice it to say that many of the game's core mechanics and moments are reflected in it. Some scenes even feel pulled straight from the game.

Of course, this is partly because both Kinetic's game and Boyle's film draw on real-life theories about ghosts and how to interact with them, rather than the movie intentionally cribbing the game's core identity. Still, it made me wonder how the eventual Phasmophobia movie might handle some similar situations. 

Never After Dark is in theaters across the US right now, albeit in limited release, so check that it's playing near you. Alternatively, you could also stream it at home soon. I haven't seen any announcement about whether it'll end up on any subscription service, but its rent-at-home premiere is set for October 28, making it a smart choice for Halloween weekend if you feel like you've seen everything scary and need something new.

I went into the movie because I'd heard about its nearly perfect aggregate review score and because I thought it might feel like something from my favorite director, Kiyoshi Kurosawa. It definitely checked that box, I'm happy to say, but just as central to its vibe is a fascinating look at what a Phasmophobia movie might look like--before we get the real thing in the (hopefully near) future.

title: After Beating Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Help Dracula Rebuild In This Awesome Roguelike
summary:
Let’s face it, if you are a Castlevania fan or just love metroidvania games in general, you’re probably sinking your teeth into Belmont’s Curse. And why not? After all, it just got a glowing review from our own Steve Watts, and like plenty of the rest of you, I’ve also been eagerly waiting for a new Castlevania adventure for over a decade. One indie team in particular seems keen to grab your attention once your time with Belmont's Curse is over, having recently released a demo for their Castlevania-adjacent roguelike. That game is Draftula, which asks, "What if Dracula commissioned you to build his labyrinthine castle?"

Draftula’s demo is available on Steam for everyone to try right now. It plays like a deckbuilder, but instead of collecting cards, you earn tile pieces that are castle rooms. The goal of each run is to place each room tile in such a way that you build a castle tall enough to prevent the vampire hunter from knocking it down at the end of the night. You can also inhabit each room with monsters, which can further slow the vampire hunter down. Each piece has a coin cost so you need to be strategic in how you construct Dracula's castle, and depending on your performance each run, you can earn hearts that can be spent between runs to unlock permanent upgrades.

It may sound easy, but the catch is that Dracula’s powers are somewhat weakened; he’s just woken up from a long slumber. Because of his diminished capabilities, you can't just immediately build the castle as a tower--to overcome certain height restrictions, you'll be required to use specific tiles to break the wards blocking you. Runs can conclude as quickly as several seconds or take as long as a few minutes, depending on which rooms and monsters show up and how much gold you can earn with each tile placement in order to place more rooms or monsters. 

Of course, all of this is in vain. After each night, a heroic knight named Sir Del Montes ruthlessly tears down Dracula’s newly built castle. Players will then go to the hub area: a cliff overlooking the building site, where Dracula and various vendors reside. Some of these vendors sell new castle pieces for the hearts you collect over multiple runs, which in turn open opportunities to expand the castle beyond its current limits. Some building pieces are given temporarily, such as the one in the current demo build: the innkeeper, who wants his room surrounded by at least five other tiles. Del Montes even has some gentle words of encouragement for you, though he also says that he’ll knock down whatever you put up!

So far, almost every part of Draftula is meticulously calculated, from the roster of available parts to its pleasing retro vibe and chill music. The demo isn't very long, consisting of only a handful of runs before the lack of available room tiles halts progression--you just can't reach the next height requirement. However, of what's there, Draftula feels like a roguelike that rewards planning, and I hope the full game expands on its awesome gameplay loop.

My one big criticism is that Draftula needs an undo button just in case you make a mistake. It can be frustrating to accidentally misclick where I wanted a tile to go, so hopefully a way to circumvent that will be included in the full game. 

But don't let my one complaint put you off trying out the game; the Draftula demo is great and it's only getting better. The demo has just been updated with a new Nightly mode, for example. This update adds a set number of tiles, a map, and mods that change the rules. These include bonuses that are granted whenever you place a room, such as randomly putting an Evil Eye room (which re-adds all other rooms in its row back to your available pieces) on the board after every fourth room you place, not being able to place more rooms in the same column of space during the turn you already placed a room there, and randomly distributing a copy of one room you’ve just played.

The scoring method in Nightly mode is also predetermined, with bonuses calculated for the number of rooms placed, the castle’s height, and any coins and gems earned for that run. It’s a good way to keep practicing before the game’s release. You can retry as many times as you like, but you can only submit your score to the leaderboard once. 

There’s currently no release date set for Draftula. However, if you fancy a chill construction game on theme with the latest Castlevania adventure, or just need a break from its many difficult boss battles, consider giving this demo a go!

title: How To Get Minior In Pokemon Go
summary:
A new Pokemon is landing soon in Pokemon Go. The meteorite Minior is making their debut in the mobile game beginning October 19, but you won't encounter them like a typical Pokemon.

Rather than periodically spawning in the wild, Minior's appearance is fittingly tied to meteor showers. The celestial Pokemon will only spawn on certain evenings when a real-world meteor shower is taking place, so you'll need to fire up the game on specific nights if you want to catch a glimpse of the new monster.

To help you add the falling star to your collection, here are some tips on how to catch Minior, including a schedule of upcoming meteor showers, how to change Minior's form, and whether the meteorite Pokemon can be shiny.

In This Article
  • How To Get Minior
  • Minior Shower Schedule
  • How To Change Minior's Form
  • Can Minior Be Shiny?

How To Get Minior

Minior is a little different from other common Pokemon in that they won't just randomly spawn in the wild; you'll only have a chance to encounter one on evenings when a meteor shower is taking place.

During these specific nights, Minior will spawn on the map between 5 PM and 11:59 PM local time. From there, it's simply a matter of waiting for one to appear, then tapping on them to initiate a catch encounter. You can increase your odds of successfully catching the Pokemon by first feeding them a Razz Berry.

Minior Shower Schedule

Minior will appear in the wild during the following meteor showers:

Orionids

  • October 19
  • 5-11:59 PM local time

Leonids

  • November 14
  • 5-11:59 PM local time

Geminids

  • December 11
  • 5-11:59 PM local time
  • One Minior color will debut in the Northern Hemisphere, and another color will debut in the Southern Hemisphere

Eta Aquariids

  • May 3
  • 5-11:59 PM local time

Southern Delta Aquariids

  • July 28
  • 5-11:59 PM local time

Perseids

  • August 10
  • 5-11:59 PM local time

According to the official Pokemon Go website, a different Minior core color will debut during each of the aforementioned events, so you'll need to play the game during every meteor shower if you're hoping to add all seven core colors to your collection.

A couple of bonuses will also be available during the meteor shower events. You'll receive extra Stardust for catching Minior, and you'll see shooting stars streaking across the in-game sky from 5-9 PM local time. The game will also offer a free Timed Research that rewards you with a Star Piece and additional Stardust when completed.

How To Change Minior's Form

Minior doesn't evolve into any other Pokemon, but the meteorite Pokemon does come in several different variants. 

Every Minior you encounter will initially be in Meteor Form, with the same brown outer shell. Once the Pokemon sustains enough damage during battle and their HP drops below 50 percent, their shell will break to reveal a different colored core.

There are seven core colors in total, one for every hue of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. One core color will debut during each meteor shower.

Can Minior Be Shiny?

At the moment, shiny Minior is not yet available in Pokemon Go. Shiny variants are typically introduced several months after a Pokemon first makes their debut, so shiny Minior may arrive down the line as part of some future event. However, nothing has been announced yet.

We're coming up on the end of October, but Pokemon Go still has a few events lined up for this month, including its annual Halloween celebration. You can see everything going on in the mobile game over the next few days in our October events roundup.

title: WoW: Forever Is Soaring, But Midnight Is Struggling
summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever is riding high thanks to its popular beta and upcoming launch, but retail WoW's Midnight expansion feels like it's in a state of crisis by comparison.

The two different versions of WoW couldn't be in more different places. Forever seems to be extremely popular, with Blizzard developers commenting how its beta is breaking records. Blizzard itself has also been more communicative regarding Forever than ever before, with weekly podcasts diving into community topics, forum posts addressing various issues, and frequent updates addressing balance problems and bugs.

Midnight seems to be in the opposite corner. Its latest content update, patch 12.1.5, went live October 13. In addition to new story quests that continue the expansion's main narrative, it added a new single-boss raid and a long-teased mega delve (officially called a labyrinth) that gives solo-focused players an almost raid-like experience.

Unfortunately, the patch was released in a bug-riddled state. The Kindo'jan labyrinth, arguably the patch's biggest feature, saw players running into issue after issue. Some players complained about not earning credit for boss kills and being unable to collect rewards. One particularly nasty bug had players falling through the floor of the labyrinth's final boss arena, making it so the labyrinth couldn't be completed. Other players cited issues with delve companion Valeera dying too quickly or failing to do proper boss mechanics.

Many of the most glaring bugs (like falling through the floor) were fixed in a hotfix deployed on October 16, but labyrinths still have a major issue: no save points. When Blizzard first detailed labyrinths, it implied players would be able to start one, make some progress, and come back to finish it at a later time. Blizzard's exact wording was that players would be able to "venture through them in a single epic session or tackle them piece by piece over time, progressing at your own pace." 

That currently isn't true, as the labyrinth has no checkpoints and must be completed in a single session. Labyrinths taking at least an hour or so to complete, combined with various bugs preventing progress and no way to save and come back to them later, is making for an incredibly frustrating experience. It's unclear if the lack of checkpoints is a bug, an unannounced change on Blizzard's part, or just some kind of oversight, but it's not a great debut for Midnight's newest feature.

Story spoilers for WoW: Midnight patch 12.1.5 below.

Bugs and issues surrounding labyrinths are just one part of why patch 12.1.5 has proven unpopular. The patch is also catching flak for its story, specifically how it killed off a major character unceremoniously. Liadrin, a blood elf paladin and one of the main characters players have interacted with over the course of Midnight, dies facing off against Kithix, the resurrected Old God general that serves at the patch's new raid encounter. 

However, she doesn't die in any kind of epic or heroic way. Instead, judging from the post-raid cinematic, she dies from what seems to be exhaustion, having wielded the power of the light too strongly in the battle against Kithix. After Kithix's defeat, Liadrin utters "Darkness will never prevail" before crumpling to the ground and dying.

WoW is not a stranger to having major characters die. It famously happened with Varyian Wrynn, the leader of the Alliance, during the start of the game's Legion expansion. But unlike Varyian's epic death, Liadrin's feels anticlimactic. The fact that it occurs during a .5 patch that feels disconnected to the game's larger narrative makes the story beat feel unnecessary. 

Adding salt to the wound is that her death looks to be in service of a recurring and unpopular trend in recent WoW storylines where old rivalries and feuds between factions are easily reconciled. In Liadrin's case, her death brings together the blood elves and the Amani trolls, though Blizzard does make a point in a post-raid quest to emphasise the two groups are not allies despite now being at peace. Blizzard may have said its putting the "war" back in Warcraft during BlizzCon 2026, but all of its recent story beats have seen ancient enemies coming together and cooperating, and Liadrin's death only serves to reinforce that.

title: You Don’t Need An Expensive Console Or High-End PC To Play Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4
summary:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 releases this week, and with gaming consoles and capable PC rigs now more expensive than ever, you might be wondering if there is another way to play.

Thankfully, there is, but there are a few things you need to know before jumping in.

How to play MW4 without a console or PC

With Game Pass:

Modern Warfare 4 is not included with Xbox Game Pass this year, but if you're a subscriber you can leverage the "stream your own game" program to play it that way, after purchasing it outright.

This isn't locked away to any specific tier of Game Pass, either. You can subscribe to Game Pass Essential, Premium, or Ultimate to stream MW4.

With GeForce Now:

Nvidia's streaming service, GeForce Now, will be another way to play Modern Warfare 4 without any expensive hardware like a new console or high-end PC. Or at least we think so. Nvidia hasn't outright confirmed this, but people are playing the campaign early access via GeForce Now, so it stands to reason that it will be officially supported at launch for everyone.

After buying the game outright, you'll be able to stream MW4 on GeForce Now by subscribing to one of the platform's membership tiers.

GeForce Now has multiple tiers, including a free ad-supported membership. There are also $10/month and $20/month tiers with no ads and higher-fidelity experiences. There are also day passes available.

For more, check out the GeForce Now website.

Pros and cons of streaming

Before subscribing to Game Pass or GeForce Now, people should know that playing a twitch shooter like Modern Warfare 4 over the internet might not always be the perfect experience. After all, a cloud service works best with a strong and stable connection, and that's not always a guarantee. However, many people report good experiences, and as always, your mileage may vary.

Something else to consider is that, starting in November, Microsoft will implement caps on how many hours people can stream via Game Pass before they must pay more to keep playing.

The benefits of streaming are pretty obvious: You don't need any expensive hardware. This is because a game is streamed on high-end hardware and beamed to your screen, whatever that may be. You will still need a controller or a keyboard and mouse setup, but you might have those things already, and if you don't, they cost significantly less than a new console or a powerful PC.

Why are consoles and PCs so expensive today?

The Xbox Series X|S and PS5 consoles were released in 2020, but today, six years later, they are more expensive than ever. Historically, console prices come down instead of going up. So what's driving the price increases? The AI-fueled demand for components and memory is to blame, as is the war in Iran that's driving up oil prices. There are numerous other macroeconomic factors at play, too, including tariffs.

Companies like Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo want to keep making money in this environment. Instead of eating the costs (while they make huge profits and collect tariff refunds), they are charging people more to maintain their margins.

The Switch 2 is among the cheapest ways to play MW4 this year, with that console starting at $500 (up from $450 at launch). The PS5 now starts at $600 (up from $400 at launch) and the latest Xbox consoles are more expensive, too. The Series S now goes for $500 (was $300) and Series X for $750 ($500 at launch). In short, you're in for major sticker shock if you're buying a new console.

For PC players, it's more expensive than ever to build a capable rig, but your price will vary depending on the setup you want, preconfigured or made yourself.

For more, check out GameSpot's Modern Warfare 4 campaign review, and keep checking back for more coverage on DMZ and multiplayer when the game goes live on October 23.

title: This LA Noire Spinoff Idea Sounds Incredible
summary:
British actor Rahul Kohli (Saros, Midnight Mass) has a pitch for a new L.A. Noire game, and it sounds pretty great. Speaking to BAFTA Games, Kohli said he would like to see the franchise return with a spinoff that takes players through different time periods, as a cop, as they investigate different crimes.

One such setting could be Victorian England, with a storyline focused on hunting down Jack the Ripper, Kohli said. Another could take players to the '80s in California as they pursue the Night Stalker, the actor added.

"We could jump around and be a cop in different times. I would be down for that," Kohli said. "I loved it. I adored L.A. Noire."

In particular, Kohli said he was a big fan of developer Team Bondi's facial-capture system which created lifelike expressions in the game, down to granular details like how a person’s eyebrows might move.

In a game where players had to read people's facial expressions, this was a big deal, and one can only imagine how much further the technology could go today. However, Kohli said he wants a new L.A. Noire game with the same tech and the same engine.

"I want that. I don't want an improvement to it. That was part of the charm," he said.

L.A. Noire was released in 2011. It never got a sequel, and its developer, Team Bondi, later disbanded. A virtual reality game, L.A. Noire: The VR Case Files, was released in 2017.

Earlier this year, Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick said the company was looking at future projects in all of its franchises, and that includes L.A. Noire.

Back in 2012, Rockstar said a sequel to L.A. Noire was a “possibility.” At the time, the developer said, “We don’t always rush to make sequels, but that does not mean we won’t get to them eventually. We have so many games we want to make, and the issue is always one of bandwidth and timing.”

Recently, a rumor emerged that a new L.A. Noire game is now in the works, and it will have players collecting clues to try to find the Zodiac Killer.

title: Saros Gets Boss Rush And Tons Of Difficulty Options With Zenith Update
summary:
Saros is a phenomenal sci-fi shooter, and it currently stands as my favorite game of 2026. If you've been waiting for the right time to play it--or to play it again--then developer Housemarque has some good news. The new Zenith update is now available for free, adding a boss rush and difficulty options that should appeal to both newcomers and seasoned veterans.

First up, the boss rush. Dubbed "Overlord Rush," the mode comes with its own dedicated leaderboards and tasks you with taking out a series of the game's bosses. Rather than starting on the first boss and fighting uninterrupted to the very end, they're divided into separate "sets" that each contain three fights. Overlord Rush is available via the Primary robot in the main hub area.

The new settings and difficulty modifiers, meanwhile, allow you to both reduce and increase the game's challenge, customizing it to fit your preferences. The "Slow Game Speed" setting lets you slow down the entire game so you have more time to react to projectiles, and you can tweak exactly how much it slows down and even if you want it to turn on automatically when combat starts. An "Auto-fire" setting also eliminates the need to actually pull the trigger when you aim, which can be handy when you're primarily focused on dodging incoming attacks. You can think of it almost like a Vampire Survivors-style tool.

Carcosan Modifiers were already in the game at launch, giving you the choice to make the game easier or harder--or a mix of both in different parts of the game--but a whole bunch more were added with Zenith. New Protection modifiers include a "Corruption Melee Enhancement," as outlined on the PlayStation Blog, which gives your melee attacks more power if you acquire Corruption, which is typically not a good thing to have.

Trial Modifiers, meanwhile, make the game more challenging, and when combined with the new ultra-hard endgame Eclipse Layers, you'll be able to put all your skills to the test.

Saros is available exclusively on PS5. In our Saros review, Richard Wakeling called it an "incredible game that does more than just refine what worked before."

title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer’s Biddy Blas Is Voiced By A Sinister Circus Ringmaster Pro Wrestler, And This Makes Sense
summary:
Star Wars has had no shortage of breakout alien stars over the decades--from Chewbacca in the original trilogy to Grogu from The Mandalorian--but in Star Wars: Galactic Racer, that honor belongs to Biddy Blas. Who is Biddy Blas? A hotshot racer in the game, with an ego the size of a Death Star and a voice that sounds like a TIE Fighter fueled by nightmares—that's who Biddy Blas is. And in real life, the man behind the voice is none other than indie UK wrestler and actor Richard Summers-Calvert, who is down to "scrib doon" some autographs from fans.

Performing under the name "The Spectacular Tw*t" Charles Crowley, Summers-Calvert has popped up in multiple pro wrestling promotions, including a recent appearance in Ring of Honor. The actor and wrestler says he's been humbled by Biddy Blas's popularity since he was introduced in Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

"I could tell Biddy Blas was gonna be popular early on," Summers-Calvert said to Soundsphere. "Then I woke up the next day and he'd blown up a bit, and then the next day it kind of dawned on me that this isn’t normal."

Since then, Summers-Calvert says he has received a ton of messages, mentions, and even "Biddy Blas thirst traps" online. For the role, Summers-Calvert recalled that the audition called for a small man who was constantly on the edge and overcompensating, which convinced the pro wrestler to raise his pitch. The game directors liked it, but the role wasn't easy--especially when he had to perform his lines in the Star Wars language of Huttese. "I keep seeing online people talking about like cuteness aggression, and they love him so much they want to throw him at the wall," Summers-Calvert added.

The popularity of Biddy Blas has only grown in recent weeks, as the character has been referenced in numerous memes and even by sports teams, like the Pittsburgh Steelers:

For pro wrestling fans, it's another example of how the theatrical side of sports entertainment has naturally connected with video games. Roman Reigns, who plays Akuma in the new Street Fighter movie, recently commented on the power of video games and how performers prefer to spend their downtime between shows with a console. Other wrestlers like Kenny Omega have also incorporated video games into their movesets and personas, referencing their favorite titles as signature attacks in the ring. At this rate, don't be too surprised if a Wrestler starts hitting his opponents with the "Scrib Doon" finisher.

If you haven't checked it out yet, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is now available for PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S. It's pretty great, blending Burnout- and Wipeout-inspired speed with a well-designed roguelite core that makes every race feel challenging and dangerous.

title: Star Wars Games Could Get More Interesting As Lucasfilm Looks Beyond The Big Studios
summary:
This year has seen the launch of two Star Wars games, with each one offering a new take on a galaxy far (far!) away. Bit Reactors' Star Wars Zero Company puts its best XCOM foot forward with an aggressive take on turn-based tactics, while Fuse Games' Star Wars Galactic Racer has been hailed for its superb roguelite racing, slick presentation, and the delightful Biddy Blas. Both games have been well received by critics and fans alike, and Lucasfilm Games has been paying attention to the success these independent studios have achieved.

"It very much is part of the strategy," Lucasfilm Games VP Douglas Reilly said to The Game Business Show. "Obviously, huge AAA games like Battlefront are always going to be an essential part of the strategy. But one of the great things about Star Wars is it has all kinds of other opportunities to tell stories in different genres. The goal has been to find the best partner to bring that experience to life inside the galaxy far, far away. And it doesn’t have to always be AAA; sometimes it can be AA, and it’s really about the experience that we’re delivering and the fantasy we’re fulfilling."

Reilly added that Lucasfilm Games wants to be more flexible in choosing who it partners with to create more Star Wars titles, and some of those studios will "surprise" people when they're eventually revealed. As Reilly put it, Lucasfilm Games isn't looking for a "top five publisher," but rather teams that can meet their expectations for a high-quality title.

title: Open-World Crime Game Samson Did Better On Console But Not Enough To Save Its Developer From Shutting Down
summary:
Liquid Swords, the Swedish developer behind the crime game Samson, is closing up shop. Founder Christofer Sundberg confirmed this after bankruptcy reports emerged, stating directly, "Liquid Swords is closing."

Samson launched on PC in April, but the console edition for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S that released in September "did far better," Sundberg said. However, he admitted that, "It wasn't enough to save the studio."

At the same time, Samson might have a future after Liquid Swords closes up shop, the executive said.

"I’m proud of our team and what we built. We’re discussing continued support for Samson. We make mistakes, we learn, we rise, we move on. I never give up. More soon," he wrote.

According to a report, all 27 employees at Liquid Swords are being let go as part of the bankruptcy process. Workers reported not getting paid for two months, but those salaries will be covered by local laws in Sweden.

Liquid Swords described itself as a "zero-nonsense" game studio. Sundberg said, "Game development has become so full of distractions that affect quality and motivation." He said his ambition was to "change that" with Liquid Swords through eliminating crunch and "useless" meetings, and not taking on an "unnecessary stakeholders."

In the end, this plan did not work out, and Samson will be Liquid Swords' one and only release.

Sundberg co-founded Just Cause studio Avalanche and spent more than a decade there before leaving to start Liquid Swords. Sundberg is known for his hot takes on the gaming industry, including a very bleak outlook on the state of gaming today.

title: Control Resonant Is Everything The First Game Wasn’t, And That’s Why It Works
summary:
With the recently released Control Resonant, Remedy Entertainment returns to its weird Control universe of teleporting toy ducks, nightmarish creatures, and explosive action, all of which is grounded by a deeply personal central story. But when considering its predecessor, Control, I was struck by just how much this sequel not only differs from the first game, but deliberately inverts or twists what players previously experienced--much as the central Big Bad does to the entire borough of Manhattan. 

Control Resonant begins with our protagonist Dylan, barefoot and in dire need of a shave, awakening from a seven-year coma. With his sister--the series' former main character, Jesse Faden--missing and Control's Oldest House now a crime scene of corpses, Dylan finally leaves the building he’s been imprisoned in for over two decades. He finds a mostly empty Manhattan, cut off from the world, along with the remnants of the FBC, which Dylan deduced was trying to fight the Hiss and a strange, new apocalyptic entity: the Patterning.

Dylan, trained in melee combat, must use his powers and abilities to find his sister and put an end to this world-ending catastrophe. 

Yet perhaps the most significant subversion in Resonant is how Jesse and Dylan's roles--one a savior, the one needing to be saved--are reversed. According to developer  Remedy, this was an intentional decision that is reinforced throughout the game.

In a recent interview with creative director Mikael Kasurinen, he told me that the first decision Remedy made with Resonant was making Dylan the protagonist. He immediately noted the contrast between the siblings.

“Dylan is from the paranatural world,” he said, “and Jesse is from our world. Their journeys need[ed] to be from one to another.”

The contrasts continue: Jesse uses a shape-changing gun, and Dylan a shape-changing rod; Jesse spent her life trying to track down the FBC while Dylan longed to escape it; Jesse becomes the head of the FBC and is greeted as the hero the bureau needs, while Dylan is its number-one enemy, often mocked--even to his face--as the regrettable Plan B for the FBC; Control is set almost entirely inside the Oldest House, while Resonant takes to the streets.

Jesse, a lifelong drifter with a leather jacket, is filled with confidence and “ready to become the director of the FBC.” In the first game, she even remarks, “Everything here is crazy. Weird. But it feels … right. Like how the world should be.”

In contrast, Kasurinen said, “Dylan is lacking confidence; he feels worthless because of his past and personal failures.” Dylan blames himself for the initial destruction seen in the first game, after he willingly let the Hiss take over his body as he yearned for freedom from the lifetime of torture to which the FBC subjected him. Unlike his sister, Dylan doesn't at all feel like he's found himself during his time in the Oldest House.

Despite opposite journeys, Kasurinen stressed that “the emotional impact is the same,” highlighting how the Faden siblings share being “fish out of water.”  

In Control Resonant, Dylan's sense of alienation is heightened by its surreal, ever-changing environments. When players step into Manhattan, the world is fractured and broken, but not destroyed. The Patterning divides Manhattan into mirrored projections of itself, inverting angles and gravity. Buses curve over roads that suddenly become vertical. Buildings split into mirror images. This is the Patterning, rearranging the entire world that Dylan must contend with.

However, and as art director Elmeri Raitanen was quick to note, the Patterning is not about destruction.

“One key aspect to us in the design philosophy was that the Patterning doesn't destroy things,” Raitanen said. “It doesn't rip pipes off the ground, shatter roads, or crack building facades. But things … exist in multiple places simultaneously.” 

Instead, the Patterning creates a simultaneous existence, in which structures are layered atop or next to each other. This phenomenon is part of what makes Resonant's world design unique. It’s why you see people with four limbs or two faces, as the Patterning’s effect is layers, not erosion. It’s why buildings “fold,” or spread.

Dylan eventually becomes really the only person that can navigate this world. He can walk up walls, scale to the top of buildings, and even glide over gaps.

I asked the team what particular artists or designs inspired this world, and they named the Padovan Sequence--a math sequence that has a “recurrence relation”--MC Escher's works, and a Donald Duck comic.

Lead level designer Anne-Marie Grönroos said that the comic “A Matter of Some Gravity” was a "great inspiration.” In that story, Donald and Uncle Scrooge are cursed by a spell that changes their personal gravity: They can walk on walls or fall sideways, while everyone else is unaffected. Anyone who’s played Control Resonant knows exactly what this feels like, as same as his feathered inspirations, Dylan can also walk up walls and fall horizontally. “We wanted to capture that same feeling of surprise and revelation when your [individual] gravity gets shifted,” Grönroos said.

Shifting the Control series' setting from the FBC--an agency that reacts to killer fridges the same way you and I do cold coffee--to Manhattan also meant the team could show the impact Altered Items, the term Remedy uses to refer to ordinary items imbued with paranormal powers,  have on normal people. This was yet another way to juxtapose these two stories, Grönroos noted, with Resonant's “mundane backdrop [making] the weirdness stand out more.” 

In the game, you'll find ordinary people at a house party with a possessed karaoke machine that refuses to let them stop dancing for days on end. At another location, a woman is convinced her twin is actually a living plant. The Oldest House, unlike Manhattan, was designed to deal with the weird. Manhattan and its people were not. Dylan, however, is fully trained, making him the right person for a world gone wrong.

But Dylan isn’t alone. He finds a friend in his handler, Zoe de Vera, who becomes the voice in his--and the player’s--ear. Kasurinen said it was important that Dylan, unlike his sister, not have his inner monologue communicated. “I wanted to hide his thoughts so that we focus on how he communicates with others,” he said. “The game is a lot about trust and connection, and Dylan wants to connect.”

This again speaks to the differences between the characters. “Whereas Jesse needed [a being called Polaris], a paranatural guide in a paranatural world,” Kasurinen said, “Dylan needed a human guide in the human world. Both needed a representative of both realities to help them understand that realm better.”

Kasurinen also noted another important distinction between the siblings thatI hadn't considered: Dylan and Jesse’s relationship to the enemy bosses, who were once human. Jesse seems to feel very little for the big corrupted entities she fights: They were, after all, part of the agency that had kidnapped her brother.

But in Resonant, we're often led through the life of the ordinary person who the Patterning changes into an often gigantic monstrous entity. We encounter an artist who had moved to New York with her mother; a physicist who’s lost contact with his family; a deserter from the FBC, terrified of what he’s seen.

I felt sympathy for these innocent people who were suddenly corrupted by this powerful force. Dylan himself shows pity, sometimes refusing to land a final blow, and remarking to others that these entities were once people. As Kasurinen explained it:

“We might see a monster, but Dylan sees a victim because that’s how he ultimately feels about himself."

Just as a supernatural force took over their bodies, this is the same as “what happened to Dylan when he was taken over by Hiss in [Control].”

Finally, I wanted to know more about Casper Darling, the previous head of research at the FBC for whom I developed very strong negative feelings in Resonant.

Although Darling was presented in a more charming manner in Control--chirpy, happy, intelligent, and driven by a need to make machines that save lives--we come to discover he was largely responsible for Dylan’s kidnapping and torturous mistreatment. Darling was rightfully convinced that they needed a way to combat bigger threats, and he, also correctly, noted Dylan had developed incredible powers. Indeed, it was Dylan, not Jesse, who was supposed to become head of the FBC, as Darling had sought to “train” him.

But while we know from the first game that Darling was closely involved in Dylan's detention, it's only in Resonant, when Dylan returns to his prison, that we find the full extent of Darling's complicity, shading the fan-favorite character in much darker hues. Gone is the sense that he's a lovably nerdy scientist sticking out like a radiant buoy among a sea of bureaucrats. Darling is a bully, a physical and emotional abuser; he ignores Dylan’s cries for help, like he ignores Dylan's obvious abuse at the hands of another angry adult. “As he tried to make Dylan be what [Darling] thought he should be,” Kasurinen said, “the failure and mistakes surfaced [Darling’s] worst instincts.” He said that “what we see of Darling is often a façade,” contrasting Darling with Dylan, who “everyone sees as a monster.”

Yet again, more contrast. “A big theme in the game was that we shouldn’t judge a book by its cover,” Kasurinen told me. In the case of Dylan, that was true in the traditional sense--that he is a more sympathetic character than perhaps some once thought. But for Darling, the opposite comes into focus, leaning into Remedy's decades-old obsession with nominative determinism, only now flipping even that on its head in Resonant. He is no "darling." He's an unempathetic scientist, resorting to whatever means he deems necessary to achieve his desired end. 

For Remedy's often obsessive fans, it's a fascinating wrinkle. It's not a heel turn for the doctor. We're catching up with his past. He was already like this when players met him in 2019's game; we just hadn't seen it yet. It's stomach-turning to reconcile those earlier feelings about Darling with this newer, fuller view of his character.

Indeed, as you play Resonant, the monsters we kill, the humans we trust, and the world we know peel back to reveal something else beneath--something that often defies the first game's aesthetic, themes, and even what we once understood to be established truths. One of the reasons Resonant terrifies me more than a lot of horror games is just how Remedy reaffirmed how little we truly know and, therefore, how much we cannot control.

title: Battlefield 6 Dev Owns Up To Mistakes With Strange-Looking Cosmetics, But Stays Silent On Possible AI Use
summary:
Battlefield Studios has released a statement regarding Battlefield 6 after players came together to point out oddities and irregularities with some of the game's newest cosmetics, leading many to openly wonder whether they were the result of generative AI.

The developer’s statement admits mistakes with some of the newly released cosmetics, but it did not say whether genAI played a role.

Battlefield Studios said it's aware of the "conversation, memes, and candid feedback" about some of Battlefield 6's new skins and cosmetic items. In particular, fans pointed out that a McNeil skin says "SECUTY" on the shoulder instead of "SECURITY." Battlefield Studios is planning to release an update to address this with the Season 5, Phase 2 patch in November.

"However, we recognize that letting a known visual error go live without quick acknowledgement creates confusion and erodes trust. We are reviewing how we communicate known visual bugs so you aren’t left wondering whether something was intentional or overlooked," the developer said.

Battlefield Studios went on to say it takes pride in "the craft of our world and our gear," and acknowledged that this item missed the mark and does not reflect the developer's own quality standards.

"Seeing visual oddities slip through is frustrating for everyone. We are currently examining our internal processes and workflows to pinpoint how these issues occurred and to see how we can tighten our quality control process going forward," the developer said.

Battlefield Studios also addressed the Midnight Mirage skin design that gives the character five pistols--you can see this below.

The developer said this was an intentional creative choice to reflect the "over-the-top action movie tropes" where soldiers inexplicably always seem to have another weapon strapped to their gear.

"That said, we understand how this could look unintentional when released alongside other cosmetic anomalies. As we continue to try out new ideas to see what interests the community, you help us continue to evolve our cosmetics in Battlefield. Thank you for your continued feedback and support," the studio said.

When Battlefield 6 launched in 2025, people immediately spotted what they thought were AI-created assets, and Battlefield Studios never denied this. The higher-ups at Battlefield Studios are big believers in AI for game development.

While Battlefield Studios may not have acknowledged using AI for in-game assets in Battlefield 6, Activision freely admits to using the technology to create some of its own assets, including with the upcoming Modern Warfare 4.

Brandon Stirrup, who works on the business strategy team at Microsoft for Xbox, said recently that companies using AI in 2026 in their workflows is standard practice across numerous industries, including gaming. He said gamers express "negative sentiment" about it, so developers don't always freely admit to using the tech. "Everyone else accepts reality," he said.

In other Battlefield 6 news, the game was recently added to Xbox Game Pass, and it's marked down on all platforms to celebrate the recent Season 5 launch.
